# SK6032 — An abstract type declares nothing to implement

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

`abstract` says both "do not instantiate this" and "a derived type completes it", and a class with no hooks, nothing `protected` and no base is only saying the first.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Design |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Syntax |
| Needs a compilation | no |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| Supersedes | S1694 |

## Why

A reader who meets `abstract class Report` expects to find the part a subclass has to supply, and goes looking for it. When there is no `abstract` member, no `virtual` member, nothing `protected` and no base type, there is nothing to find: no derived type is required to provide anything, none is offered anything it could not get from an instance, and the keyword's only effect is that `new Report()` does not compile. That is a real intent and there are three better ways to state it — a `static` class if the members are all static, an interface if the members are all contracts, or a concrete class if instantiating it is fine — and each of the three tells the next reader something. `abstract` alone tells them to keep looking for a hook that is not there.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
public abstract class Endpoints {
    public static string Health => "/health";

    public static string Ready => "/ready";
}
```

Write:

```csharp
public static class Endpoints {
    public static string Health => "/health";

    public static string Ready => "/ready";
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **The `protected` exemption is the one carrying the rule, and a protected constructor is its usual form.** A base class that shares state through a `protected` constructor, a `protected` field or a `protected` helper is arranged for derivation whether or not it declares anything abstract, and reporting it would be reporting the most ordinary base class in C#. `virtual` is exempt for the same reason and counts as much as `abstract`: "you may override this" is an extension point somebody put there deliberately, and a visitor base whose every method is an empty `virtual` is the canonical shape of one. What is left after those two exemptions is a class with public and private concrete members, no base and no derived-only surface at all.

⚠ **A nested type deriving from the containing type is an exemption, and the sweep found it rather than the design did.** `abstract class Shape { private Shape() { } public sealed class Circle : Shape { … } }` is how C# spells a closed hierarchy: no `abstract`, no `virtual` and nothing `protected`, because the derived types are right there in the body — the derivation surface stated as directly as it can be. The first version of the rule reported it, which was found by running the rule over its own sibling fixtures. The base list is matched on the written name rather than on a symbol, which keeps the rule syntactic and costs a miss where a nested type derives from something else sharing the container's simple name.

**A base list on the abstract class itself is an exemption on its own, and it is why the rule is syntactic.** An abstract class that derives from something may be inheriting abstract members it deliberately does not implement, or carrying interface members a derived type must supply — both are genuine things to implement, and neither is visible in this declaration. Declining every one of them removes the only question that needed a symbol, so the rule runs under `--load=loose`. The cost is a miss on a middle-of-hierarchy class that really does add nothing.

⚠ **Records are out of scope entirely.** An `abstract record` is overwhelmingly the root of a closed hierarchy, and its generated members — the copy constructor, `EqualsContract`, the printing members — are the derivation surface a hand-written class has to declare for itself. There is no shape there this rule could read as an omission, so `record` and `record struct` are not analysed at all rather than filtered later.

**`partial` is never reported.** The other part may declare the abstract member, or may not exist yet because a generator writes it — the same single exemption that keeps `SK6023` out of every source-generated codebase.

**A type carrying an attribute is exempt.** A framework that requires a base class, a generator, or a serializer reads the attribute, so the declaration's shape is not the whole story.

**An `abstract class Foo { }` with no members at all is not reported here.** That is `SK6023`'s finding, and billing one declaration twice for one omission would double it in every report.

**The shape that stays genuinely arguable** is a base class whose members are all `public` and concrete and whose author wants only to forbid `new Report()` — `abstract class Shape { public string Name { get; init; } }` with subclasses that add nothing abstract. It is reported, the author's intent is real, and a `protected` constructor — which such a class almost always has, because that is how the name gets set — takes it out of scope. The rule ships at `suggestion` because of the ones that do not.

⚠ **The implicit constructor is not a member.** An abstract class gets a compiler-generated `protected` parameterless constructor, and the rule reads *declared* members only. Counting the generated one would exempt every abstract class in the language and leave the rule matching nothing.

⚠ **No fix.** The three repairs — drop `abstract`, make it `static`, make it an interface — are three different answers to "what was this type for", each of which changes the public surface in a different direction. Guessing between them would be guessing at intent, and the finding says look at this rather than what to do.
